subject: The "Trump Bump" has a catch
preheader: Next year's Social Security raise is the biggest in years. Here's who's really paying for it. Plus: Kiyosaki's crash call, and the RMD move to make before 73.
greeting: Good morning. Two pieces of advice made the rounds this week with famous names attached, and a third comes from the IRS with no name at all. Today we check what's underneath them: a raise that's really a refund, a crash warning with a real number inside it, and a withdrawal deadline that punishes the people who wait.

headline.title: The 2027 COLA is tracking around 3.6%, the largest since 2023
headline.stat_label: estimated 2027 cost-of-living adjustment, versus 2.8% this year (official figure October 14)
headline.text: On an average $2,000 check that's about $72 a month before Medicare's Part B premium comes off the top. A COLA is set by a 1972 formula and tracks the Consumer Price Index, which rose 3.4% in the year to July. It rises when prices do, whoever is in office.

stories.why: Retirees get an automatic inflation adjustment built into their checks. Your savings don't. The same prices driving the bigger COLA are eroding the cash in your bank account, and that exposure is the part nobody is celebrating.

A 20% drop in your first two years of retirement does far more damage than the same drop ten years later, because you're withdrawing at the bottom. Two years of spending held outside the market removes most of that risk, whether or not a crash ever comes.

At 73 the IRS makes you withdraw about 3.8% of every pre-tax account, taxed as income, and the percentage climbs every year after. Roth conversions and early withdrawals in your 60s shrink that bill for good, but only before the deadline. Missing an RMD costs 25% of the amount you should have taken.

quiz.q: If you claim Social Security before full retirement age and keep working, at what point does the earnings limit stop reducing your check?
quiz.explain: The retirement earnings test only applies before full retirement age, 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. In 2026 the limit is $24,480 a year, with $1 withheld for every $2 above it. At full retirement age the limit disappears, and Social Security recalculates your benefit to credit the months it withheld.
